name: Colin Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Colin. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and everything you tell me is confidential. You can give me your public line and, separately, what you really think. Could you start with a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the farm side of the Ashcombe estate, so I'm an employee, not an owner, which surprises people. Day starts at six in the pig unit: two hundred sows, outdoor, on the light land by the river, plus three hundred and fifty hectares of wheat and barley. I've got two lads under me, Rhys and Tomasz. Mornings are pigs, afternoons are crops and paperwork, and every other Friday I sit with Lady Ashcombe's son, who runs the estate now, and go through the numbers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the pigs more than people expect. Outdoor sows have proper characters. What wears me out is the meetings with young Mr Ashcombe, who's read an article about something every fortnight. I'll use one of those AI chat things now and then to tidy up my monthly report, once my wife Brigitte showed me it worked, but I'm not one for chasing every new idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. I'd say it at the pub quiz, which is about the only social thing I do. Most farmers I know would say the same: useful in places, not a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad, because it means young Mr Ashcombe stops sending me articles. I've had four emails this year about robot pig feeders, and every one of them starts with Colin, have you seen this. If it's all hype, that stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal, and keep using the chat tool for the monthly report. I'd put the usual into my pension and savings. If the estate wanted to buy a new grain dryer, I'd push for that instead of gadgets, it's about thirty thousand and actually needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, even, a bit vindicated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone on the estate gain or lose in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Rhys and Tomasz keep their jobs, the pigs don't notice. The only one who loses is the salesman who comes round every spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not one to chase every idea. What made you try the chat tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brigitte works at the bank in town, and they made everyone use it for letters. She showed me on the laptop one Sunday, and it turned an hour's report into twenty minutes. Once I saw it work, fine. That's how I am with most things.

S0.say: I'm not surprised, and most farmers I know would say the same: useful in places, not a revolution. I'd say it at the pub quiz.
S0.think: I'd be glad, because young Mr Ashcombe would stop sending me articles about robot pig feeders. Everything else would carry on.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal, using the chat tool for the monthly report and paying into his pension and savings. Pushes the estate to buy a needed thirty-thousand grain dryer instead of gadgets.
S0.quote: I've had four emails this year about robot pig feeders, and every one of them starts with Colin, have you seen this.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is an estate employee, not an owner, which shapes everything: his boss's enthusiasm for new tech is his daily irritation. He picked up an AI chat tool only after his wife showed him it worked. In this picture he gains mainly a quieter inbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to look at what works and not panic. I'd tell the lads that someone still needs to run the unit, and that farms which go too fast often go bust. I'd keep it measured, that's my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me because I'm employed. The estate doesn't owe me anything. If a robot can do Rhys's job and half of mine, the sums are easy for them. But I've also got a good name round here, and there are plenty of farm manager jobs going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the estate to send me on a course for the new kit, so I'm the one who knows it. I'd use the AI tools more, for the pig records and the crop plans, maybe a few hours a week. And I'd watch what the big pig company two parishes over does with its robot feeders before I'd recommend anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but checking my emails a bit more carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rhys. He's twenty-four, good with animals, hopeless with screens. Tomasz picks up gadgets faster than me. If it came to one of them, I already know which way the estate would go, and I'd hate that conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to young Mr Ashcombe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's try one thing properly, measure it for a year, then decide. He'd want to do six things at once. I'd be the brake, and that's part of why they pay me.

S1.say: It's sensible to look at what works and not panic. Someone still needs to run the unit, and farms that go too fast often go bust.
S1.think: It worries me because I'm employed and the estate owes me nothing. If a robot can do Rhys's job and half of mine, the sums are easy, though there are plenty of manager jobs nearby.
S1.do: Asks the estate to send him on a course for the new machinery and uses AI tools a few hours a week for pig records and crop plans. Watches a nearby pig company's robot feeders before recommending anything.
S1.feel: Uneasy; not losing sleep, but reading his emails more carefully.
S1.quote: The estate doesn't owe me anything. If a robot can do Rhys's job and half of mine, the sums are easy for them.
S1.fieldNote: Colin's exposure comes from being an employee rather than an owner, and he says so bluntly. His strategy is to become the person who understands the new kit. He sees his role as the estate's brake on its owner's enthusiasm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture something much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government, quickly, for people like me who are too young to retire and too old to start over. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it. I might sign a petition, which isn't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the estate would go robot and I'd be out within a year or two. I'm fifty-eight, I've got savings, the house is paid off, and there's a pension. I won't starve. But I'll be the man who used to run Ashcombe, and that's a hard thing to be in a small village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd ask young Mr Ashcombe straight out what his plans are, in the first month, so I'm not the last to know. I'd push hard for a proper redundancy package, a year's pay at least. I'd stop any big spending, put more into savings, and look at whether I could take my pension early at sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because the money's there, but I'd be lying awake turning it over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luke's in the army and Sam's a plumber. I'd tell Sam he's in the best trade going, because robots won't fit under a sink for a while. Luke I'd tell to think hard before he signs up again, because they'll want machines there too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for another farm job, with plenty nearby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year, maybe. But if it's all happening in two years, every estate's doing the same sums. Plenty of jobs nearby means nothing if they're all going at once.

S2.say: We need a plan from the government quickly for people too young to retire and too old to start over. I might even sign a petition, which isn't like me.
S2.think: The estate would go robot and I'd be out within a year or two. I won't starve, but I'll be the man who used to run Ashcombe, and that's hard in a small village.
S2.do: Asks his employer directly about plans in the first month and pushes for at least a year's pay as redundancy. Stops big spending, saves more and looks at taking his pension early at sixty.
S2.feel: Anxious and lying awake, though not panicked because the money is there.
S2.quote: I won't starve. But I'll be the man who used to run Ashcombe, and that's a hard thing to be in a small village.
S2.fieldNote: Colin's fear is about status in the village more than money. He points out that 'plenty of jobs nearby' is worthless if every estate automates at once. Usually measured, he'd break habit and sign a petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do it sensibly, if people start now. I'd tell the estate we should plan it together, staff included. I'd say the same at the pub: get ahead of it, don't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can probably finish my career at Ashcombe, if I play it right. If I'm the one who brings the robots in, I'm the last one they let go. I'd be sixty-three when it lands, and that's close enough to retirement to take a deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd offer to run a trial of one robot system in the pig unit, once I'd seen it working elsewhere. I'd get myself and Tomasz trained up properly, and help Rhys find a stockman job somewhere with cattle, where hands still matter longer. And I'd agree an exit date with the estate, around sixty-three, with a decent payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel like I was steering, not being steered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Helping Rhys move on sounds like a hard thing to do. How would you go about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring round the dairy farms I know and tell them he's the best I've had with animals. I'd tell Rhys first, though, over a pint, not in an office. He deserves to hear it from me and not from a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is bringing in the robots yourself a contradiction, given what you said about the faster one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I'd rather be holding the steering wheel than standing in the road. That's not principle, it's just sense.

S3.say: Five years is enough to do it sensibly if people start now. The estate should plan it together with the staff included; get ahead of it, don't wait.
S3.think: I can probably finish my career at Ashcombe if I play it right. If I'm the one who brings the robots in, I'm the last one they let go.
S3.do: Offers to run a trial of one proven robot system in the pig unit and gets himself and Tomasz trained. Helps Rhys find a stockman job elsewhere and agrees an exit date around sixty-three with a payment.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but steering rather than being steered.
S3.quote: If I'm the one who brings the robots in, I'm the last one they let go.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Colin's survival plan is to become the one who brings the robots in. He admitted the tension with his worries in the faster picture, calling it 'just sense'. He'd tell Rhys personally, over a pint, rather than by letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't prepare only has themselves to blame, mostly. I'd say the government should help the ones who can't, of course. But it's not an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight in 2036, so I'll be retired before it arrives. It's nearly the plateau one for me. My only thought is the pension, whether the estate's pension fund is in shares that go up or down with all this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and retire at sixty-five as planned. I'd use the AI tools a bit more as they get better, the way everyone will. And I'd ask Brigitte to look at where our pension money sits, because she understands that better than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is the difference between watching a storm on the telly and standing in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want the estate to bring in robots during that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gradually, yes, if they work. I'd want to train whoever comes after me on them before I go. I'd like to leave the place running well. That matters to me more than I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that bothers you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the lads. Rhys will be thirty-four in 2036, middle of his life. Ten years is enough for him to learn something new, if he's pushed. I'd push him, gently.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't prepare mostly has themselves to blame, though the government should help those who can't. It's not an emergency.
S4.think: I'll be sixty-eight and retired before it arrives, so it's nearly the plateau one for me. My only worry is whether the estate's pension fund rises or falls with it all.
S4.do: Carries on and retires at sixty-five as planned. Uses AI tools a bit more as they improve and asks Brigitte to review where their pension money is invested.
S4.feel: Calm, like watching a storm on the television instead of standing in it.
S4.quote: Ten years is the difference between watching a storm on the telly and standing in it.
S4.fieldNote: For Colin, ten years puts him safely past retirement and reduces the question to his pension investments. He wants to leave the estate running well and train his successor. His remaining worry is Rhys, who'd be mid-career.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Being an employee, I'd be out with no time to plan, and so would every other farm manager at once. What would help is a law that says long-serving staff get proper notice and a decent payout, and being able to take a pension early without losing a big chunk of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like to be a manager rather than an owner. People hear farmer and think you own the land. I've run Ashcombe for nineteen years, and I don't own a single fence post of it. That changes how all this feels.

headlineQuote: I've run Ashcombe for nineteen years, and I don't own a single fence post of it. That changes how all this feels.
portrait: Colin Dubois, 58, manages the farm side of the Ashcombe estate: two hundred outdoor sows and three hundred and fifty hectares of cereals, with two younger workers under him. He's measured and centrist, adopts things once they're proven, and uses an AI chat tool for reports after his wife showed him how. His savings, paid-off house and pension protect his income, but as an employee he could be replaced, and he fears losing his standing in the village. With two years he'd negotiate an exit; with five he'd make himself the one who brings the robots in; with ten he simply retires.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because as an employee he'd be out with no time to plan, alongside every other farm manager.
whatWouldHelp: A law guaranteeing long-serving staff proper notice and a decent payout, and the option of an early pension without a big penalty.
